Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words concerning the statement just made by the Minister of Transport and the document he has tabled.
We all know the railway unions and the management of the two largest railway companies in Canada are now negotiating the renewal of their contracts.
All sorts of rumours are circulating at the present time-in fact, they are not just rumours, since the Minister of Transport, by the replies he gave yesterday, seemed to imply they were true-to the effect that the federal government would provide new subsidies to the C.N.R. and C.P.R. to offset the salary increase which will be granted to employees of those two large companies.
We have nothing to say against a wage increase for railway employees, on the contrary; however, we object to the government increasing its subsidies to the two railway companies concerned, because we note at the present time that the rates of those companies are much lower than those of trucking companies for the transport of similar goods. This is unfair competition, since the railway companies are using moneys granted by the federal government and the Department of Transport to cut down their rates. Taxes paid by private trucking companies are used to subsidize their competitors which can thus reduce their rates.

Indian Affairs
Mr. Speaker, this is something quite inconsistent and absurd. The private trucking industry in Canada is being jeopardized with the taxes paid by the people.
I feel that the Minister of Transport should give the house the formal assurance that there will be no further development in the granting of subsidies to railway companies until the matter is aired before the house and then referred to the committee on railways, airlines and telegraph lines.
The minister said that the MacPherson report would be considered in the fall. I suggest, however, that the Department of Transport should not grant any additional subsidies to the C.N.R. or to the C.P.R. until the standing committee on railways, airlines and telegraph lines has had an opportunity to look into this problem of cut rates.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport should take this request into consideration and he should not add to the uneasiness which prevails at the present time in the trucking industry.

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INTENSIFIED COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Indian communities will be assisted in raising their living standards and improving their economic, social and cultural life by means of an intensified community development program which will supplement present government assistance.
[Mr. Grcgoire.!
An investment of some $3,551,000 over the next three years is proposed for this aspect of Indian development, which will be conducted by the Indian affairs branch on its own and in association with various provincial and other agencies. This amount is the minimum needed for an intensive three year program. This is the price tag for the assembled skills, organizational instruments and operating techniques which constitute this new process.
In its application, the proposed community development program is designed to employ, to the greatest extent possible, all the available material and human resources in Indian communities and in each province. One of its effects will be to step up mobilization of Indian initiative and to further promote self sufficiency. One of its end results will be to accelerate transfer to Indian communities of responsibility and authority for the management of their affairs, with concurrent limitations in government controls.
In organizational terms, this program will provide one important framework for co-ordinating and enhancing the efforts of existing health, education, welfare and economic development services in Indian communities. In facilitating the development of Indian communities this program would fill a serious gap in existing programs and reduce costs in such palliative areas as welfare assistance payments.
The success of this latest self help program is expected to bring reserves closer to being self sufficient communities and thus reduce the need for reliance on relief and other welfare assistance. This will depend in large measure on the participation of the Indians themselves in efforts to improve their level of living with as much reliance as possible on their own initiative. The program makes provision for technical and other services which will help them to establish self sufficiency. It will be noted immediately that there are over 200,000 Indians in Canada, and that at the present rate of increase there will be around 250,000 in six years.
There is a requirement for a large number of persons skilled in the field of community development to work on reserves and, as the program develops, members of the Indian communities concerned will be engaged in developing local programs. In a number of cases community development workers will be engaged and directed by the department. In other cases, with the approval of Indian bands concerned, such workers will be supplied by arrangement with provincial gov-

ernments. Canada has a shortage of qualified workers in the field of community development and it is hoped that university courses in this field soon will be established. Special courses now are being arranged for departmental staff engaged in this work to study the essential philosophy and techniques involved.
The community development program is being introduced in the three stages beginning in 1964-65 and extending to 1966-67. The stage beyond 1966-67 will represent an on-going program. Although the community development process will result in many tangible improvements on reserves, the very nature of the process is such that it is impossible to spell out in advance which specific projects and services are to be undertaken first. To preserve the effectiveness of the community development process, therefore, and particularly the decision making process at the local level, it will be necessary to make a general allocation of community development funds to each region. Under this arrangement, specific allocation will be controlled by the regional supervisor in relation to emerging needs and development on particular reserves.
As a general principle the community development program will recognize that it is neither desirable nor practicable to abolish reserves. A corollary to this is that the perpetuation or worsening of conditions on reserves will not provide incentives for people to leave. Such conditions tend to have the opposite effect in reducing mobility. Community development therefore implies acceptance of reserves as Indian communities. A community development effort will need to be sustained at least until those reserves which have the necessary potential are brought to approximate social and economic parity with neighbouring non-Indian communities. Where no economic basis for the existence of a reserve can be found, the community development process can be employed equally effectively in resettling people in other areas.
In essence, the community development program represents a conscious effort by the government to guide the forces of change in the best interests of Indian communities and the country at large. It is based on recognition that in the past purely technological approaches have frequently failed to achieve the desired results or have caused unforeseen damage to people. In undertaking this program I will remain concerned not only with the economic and technical prerequisites and
Indian Affairs
consequences of change but also with its social and cultural dimensions.

The statement made by the minister is most interesting. It is impossible, of course, to deal in any detail now with the representations he has made in respect to the changes designed to improve and elevate the position of Indians within our country. Any action taken in this connection is most commendable, giving the Indians a greater and ever increasing equality of opportunity while at the same time maintaining the treaty rights which are of the essence of our relationship with them.
This is a further step along the road we were endeavouring to map out when we were sitting opposite, giving to the Indians equality with other citizens of our country, providing them with the franchise heretofore denied to them and also ensuring representation in parliament by the appointment of Senator Gladstone to the other place.
Over the years the Indians have been of particular interest to me, beginning when we first went west in the area of Fort Carlton. I have seen the Indians passing from a position of great difficulty and squalid poverty to a state of gradual improvement and I am sure the present plan will do still more to equalize that condition of citizenship which all of us in our country must establish. Discrimination was removed in law through the bill of rights. Economic opportunity was provided through rising standards and the provision of technical schools for the Indian people who are, technologically, of a high standard of ability, but who had not possessed an opportunity to advance and improve their position.
I say to the minister that the action outlined in this statement will receive the full support of the opposition, for all of us are tremendously interested in assuring that the Indian population of our country shall attain the highest possible standards. I return to what I said near the beginning of my remarks. At all times we must preserve their treaty rights which are sacred in their sight and sacred, in their view, to the maintenance of the relationship between the Indian population and the rest of Canada.
I hope that at the same time the minister is proceeding to have set up the Indian claims commission so that their historic rights, which too often over the years have been violated and diminished, shall be given the full consideration of a semi-judicial body and, where

wrongs have taken place, right will be substituted.

Mr. Speaker, there has been no formal communication between the Soviet union and the government of Canada. The foreign ministry of Japan announced yesterday that it had received a proposal from the Soviet union, and an Associated Press dispatch indicated that this proposal would be circulated to members of the United Nations. That proposal has not been received yet, but I would say that, subject to careful further examination, we would regard this proposal as an important statement in principle by the Soviet union, and particularly so because of the Canadian interest in the principles of UN peace keeping.
The Soviet proposal seems to be a restatement by the Soviet union of its position with regard to article 43 of the charter of the United Nations. The proposal as reported suggests that the Soviet union would be prepared to support the financing of a permanent peace keeping force under the auspices of the United Nations; but that there is no indication, in anything which has yet been made public, that the Soviet union is prepared to meet the financial obligations which the international court of justice says are due from the Soviet union in respect of peace keeping operations already undertaken by the United Nations.
I can assure the right hon. gentleman that if this proposal is presented to Canada formally we shall give it very careful consideration.

It was not sent there for the primary purpose of preventing an invasion, but there is no doubt that the decision to establish the United Nations peace keeping force on the 13th of March did assist very considerably in making invasion from any quarter impossible or undesirable.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: VANCOUVER

speechtext:
I thought yesterday it might be just as well if we started getting some news from home in respect of this property instead of so much from abroad. At one point it was my intention to intervene.
This property is a former Indian reserve purchased by the federal government of Canada. A large sum of money was paid to the Indians for its acquisition. It is the property of the federal government. It was used by the R.C.A.F. during the war and since, and has become surplus to their requirements at the present time. The C.B.C. indicated that it was interested in some of the property, namely five buildings in all. These are splendid concrete buildings of considerable value, and are estimated by our Department of Public Works to have an earning capacity of $200,000 annually; so they are substantial buildings.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The property has now been declared surplus, and reference was made first to the government of the province of British Columbia as to their probable requirements. I think they indicated that they had no desire to use any of the property. Then the matter was taken up with the city, and the city is interested in it, particularly the parks board of the city of Vancouver. In recent years a portion of the area was given to parks use by the city and it is the desire of the parks board-and, I think, of many of the people of Vancouver, too-to extend the park area there.
I was not present on the occasion of the visit of Mr. Ouimet to city council, though my colleague the Postmaster General was. I think Mr. Ouimet outlined to council the requirements of the C.B.C. in respect of five buildings and a requisite amount of land to be used for parking purposes. I have suggested since that it would be highly advisable for the C.B.C. to make a formal request for their requirements and the property they need. My colleague the Secretary of State is in agreement with this, and I understand that some time very soon the C.B.C. will be making that official request.
I have suggested that I would be prepared to assist in the allocation of the remainder of the property, not to the parks board of Vancouver, because we manifestly cannot deal with them, but to the city of Vancouver. I would suggest this could probably be done over an extended lease, and if it is their desire to have it used for parks purposes of course the city of Vancouver could negotiate with the parks board. speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this bill is given second reading I think we should have a fuller explanation than we have had so far. If it is not the minister's intention to speak at this time, I would certainly like to say something about it. We had considerable discussion on April 28 with regard to this matter of allowances to teen-agers between the ages of 15 and 18; in other words, those of 16 and
17	years of age. The discussion arose on that occasion over the changes in the Income Tax Act in anticipation of this legislation being passed.
The suggestion was made at that time by myself and others in this house that a simpler way of providing this assistance to the parents of Canada would be through an amendment to the Family Allowances Act extending family allowances to the age of
18	years. I still feel this suggestion should be given consideration before we go on with this bill. Therefore it seems to me this bill should be withdrawn and the government should take the other method of providing this assistance to parents of teen-agers attending school, namely by simply raising the age limit under the Family Allowances Act.
This becomes part of a larger question in Canada today, and is bound up with the efforts on the part of all Canadians to satisfy as far as they possibly can the special aspirations of the people of the province of Quebec. This was admitted by the Minister of Finance on April 28, when he was questioned about the feasibility of granting this special assistance to parents through raising the age limit under the Family Allowances Act. The Minister of Finance said this, as reported at page 2693 of Hansard:
Theoretically, I suppose, if the federal government wanted to extend the present family allowance arrangements up to the age of 18 they could do so and this would apply everywhere in Canada, including Quebec; and the government of Quebec could in that event do one of two things: It could either continue to pay its present education grants, which would mean there would be roughly twice as much paid in the province of Quebec in respect to children aged 16 and 17 as would be paid elsewhere in Canada, or alternatively, it could say: The federal government is now paying these sums; we shall stop our payments. Either of these
Youth Allowances
decisions would be perfectly logical, I suggest. However, the government of the province of Quebec says: We have been in this field for three or four years; we are doing it in a way which seems to us reasonable; a way which seems acceptable to our people, one which is well established; and we want to go on doing it that way; we would prefer it if you would pay to us the equivalent of what would have been paid by the federal government net, after income tax and so on, and if it were paid directly in respect of the children.
Anyone could argue whether or not this was a good way of doing it. As I say, the federal government could charge right ahead, ignore the fact that this is an established program in Quebec and insist on paying the amounts directly to the mothers despite the fact that the government of the province does not want this done. Or the government of Canada could say: We recognize the fact that you have been in this field for three or four years. We are not going to pay any more than the citizens of Quebec would have got under our new scheme, but instead of paying them double and embarrassing everybody we shall pay the net equivalent to the government of Quebec. And this is what will be proposed when the legislation is presented in this house.
I should like to commend the Minister of Finance for a straightforward statement of that kind; it brings the matter quite clearly into focus. But as he pointed out, anyone can argue whether or not this is the right way of doing it. As far as I am concerned, speaking on behalf of the people in the constituency of Middlesex West, I think this is not the best way of doing it. It is not the best way of doing it because of our efforts to hold this land of ours together in unity and happiness. When actions are taken by the federal government which tend in any way to divide the people of this country I think it is a mistake, and I think this legislation as proposed by the government in relation to youth allowances has this effect of dividing rather than unifying Canada.
Let us just look for a moment, Mr. Speaker, at the various clauses and provisions of Bill No. C-108. Starting with clause 2 (c), we see that young people are placed on the same basis as children under the Family Allowances Act. Clause 2 (c) (ii) says that a "dependant youth" is a person who has reached the age of 16 but is not yet 18 years of age, and-
-is, by reason of any mental or physical infirmity, precluded from attending or attending on a fulltime basis at a school or university;
Under the Family Allowances Act parents cannot collect family allowances unless their children are attending school. To put it in simple language, under the Family Allowances Act all children able to attend school should be at school. If those who are able to attend school are not at school, then their

Youth Allowances
parents are not entitled to family allowances on their behalf. Clause 2 (f) defines "parent" in this way:
"parent" means a person resident in a province other than a province providing schooling allowances who maintains a dependant youth, but does not include an institution as defined by the regulations;
In other words, the reference in this clause to a parent resident in a province other than a province providing schooling allowances means that the province concerned is the province of Quebec. Therefore these allowances cannot under this legislation be paid to parents residing in Quebec. Then clause 3 says:
Subject to this act, there may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund to a parent, in respect of a dependant youth maintained by such parent other than a dependant youth in respect of whom an allowance is payable under any law described in paragraph (h) of section 2, a monthly allowance of ten dollars.
Again we come to the idea that parents in Quebec are exempted under this legislation. These youth allowances as provided in the act cannot be paid to parents in the province of Quebec.
Although there may be some in the house who can find justification for this, I suggest that this is wrong in principle. We are treating parents in different parts of Canada differently, and I think they should all be treated alike. Therefore I submit that the government should withdraw this legislation and this assistance to the parents of children who are going to school-our teen-agers

although I admit that this legislation will otherwise be very worthy legislation for the house to pass. I am quite willing to support the government in bringing assistance to parents of 16 and 17 year old students, but this should be done through the Family Allowances Act so that all parents across the country from coast to coast, as well as their children, would be treated alike.
I am hoping that the government can see its way clear to withdraw this measure and extend family allowances. While I favour granting assistance to parents of 16 and 17 year old children, I believe it can be done in a better way through an amendment to the Family Allowances Act. I feel I should oppose this legislation in view of the fact that there is a better alternative.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the hon. member for Middlesex West, in his desire to get his remarks on the record, did not give me the opportunity to first set out the position of the government with respect to the bill. Indeed, if he had waited until he had heard the position of the government it might have changed his mind and led him not to exhaust himself on this warm afternoon.
The bill now before the house is not, as the house is well aware, an extension of the Family Allowances Act, which method of procedure was considered and for reasons which will be explained later was not followed, but is called a youth allowances bill. It is expected that hon. members will find this a more efficient way of doing what all hon. members have indicated they are desirous of doing.
Bill No. C-108, Mr. Speaker, represents a significant step forward, it is believed, in encouraging our young people to make the most of their educational opportunities. As hon. members are aware, the family allowances program, which has been in operation since 1945, provides assistance to parents of children under 16 years of age. In the 19 years since that program started the federal government has paid out more than $6J billion toward the care, maintenance, education and advancement of these younger Canadians.
But now it is felt that it is time to move forward again. It has been felt for some time that 16 and 17 year olds should also be given incentives to continue their training and education to equip them better for employment in the modem world. That, stated very briefly, is the purpose and objective of the proposed legislation.
The extra $10 a month proposed in the bill is designed to help meet the higher costs of looking after children in this particular age group. It does not, of course, begin to provide full maintenance or assistance for such children, and no one would ever suggest that it would do so. It is, however, meant to provide

an incentive to parents to persuade their children of the value of pursuing their education as far as they possibly can.
The government feels that it is money well spent to ensure that the country has an uninterrupted flow of young people coming into the labour force with the highest possible educational qualifications to meet the ever heightening demands of modern society. It represents one more advance in our continuing battle against unemployment. What is proposed in the bill is the provision of an allowance of $10 a month for the full 12 months of each year provided, of course, the youth, as defined in the bill, remains in school. Hon. members will note that in addition the government wishes to render assistance to parents of children who, by reason of a physical or mental impairment, are unable to attend school. This allowance will serve to partly close the gap for such children who, as all hon. members know, may not qualify for disability allowances until they reach the age of 18 years.
As has been pointed out, the province of Quebec has for some time had a schooling allowance program similar to the youth allowances set out in the bill. However, the Quebec provincial law provides only for a $10 allowance for each of 10 months of the year. Nor does that legislation provide for disabled children not at school. We are informed, however, that the government of the province of Quebec plan to introduce amendments which will bring their provincial program of assistance to students into line with the proposed federal program, so there will be equality in all ten provinces.
Because the province of Quebec already has its own similar program, arrangements will be made whereby instead of paying these allowances in that province, as has already been noted by the hon. member, a financial equivalent will be provided in order that the wider benefits of this bill will be available to children of the province of Quebec. All hon. members will notice that the equivalent provisions are not contained in the bill, but I am sure they will have already noted that they are contained in a resolution appearing as order No. 61 on the order paper, which deals with fiscal arrangements with the provinces.
Apart from the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, it is estimated that there are now in Canada some 502,000 persons in the age group 16 to 18, of whom some 350,000 are attending school. It is hoped that the incentive provided by the allowances may prove suf-
Youth Allowances
ficiently attractive to bring many other children back to school or otherwise cause them to pursue job or career training. Only experience will tell us how many additional children will benefit from this program, but the government hopes that large numbers will do so. Sometimes even this modest amount of assistance is enough to make the whole difference between children leaving school too early and staying on for further training.
Assuming that 375,000 children will participate initially, it is estimated that the cost to the federal government for the remaining seven months of the present year will be in excess of $27 million. This will not, of course, include the additional amount for the province of Quebec, which will be based on the number of children in that province for whom comparable provision has been made.
I should also point out, Mr. Speaker, that an important feature of this program will be to provide comparable assistance to parents who are unfortunate enough to have children in this age group who, by reason of mental or physical infirmity, are precluded from attending school or university. There are in Canada some 25,000 children aged 16 and 17 who are mentally or physically afflicted, or both. Fortunately most of them are not so disabled as to be unable to pursue their education, and they are continuing to do so.
It is estimated, none the less, that of these
25.000	children there may be 4,000 or perhaps
5.000	who will benefit from the allowance as their infirmity is such to rule out their attendance at school. The government feels it would be unfair to provide assistance to parents with children in a position to enjoy the advantages of advanced schooling and deny it to those whose children are, for physical or mental reasons, unable to do so.
As I also mentioned, this allowance will help bridge the gap to care for youngsters who are in receipt of family allowances to the age of 16 and who, under present circumstances, are unable to qualify for any further allowance until they have reached the age of 18 when they may qualify under the Disabled Persons Allowance Act.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the object of the program is to assist Canadian parents with children in the age group specified if those children are furthering their educational opportunities, as well as those who by reason of infirmity are unable to do so.
Apart from the relatively few children who are precluded from attending school, we do not propose to assist parents in supporting children who do not go to school. In other

Youth Allowances
words, Mr. Speaker, the legislation will not provide for assistance to parents of children who do not go to school for whatever personal reasons they may have. I should perhaps point out that the educational requirements of the provinces do not require any child to attend school beyond the age of 16. Some of the provinces provide even a lower age at which children may discontinue compulsory schooling. Across the land schooling is compulsory to the ages of 14, 15 or 16. It is my understanding that in British Columbia the age at which a child may leave school is 15; in Alberta it is 15; in Saskatchewan, 15; in Manitoba it is 14 and 16 depending on certain conditions which must be decided by the locality municipality; in Ontario, 16; in New Brunswick, 16; in Nova Scotia it is 14 in rural areas and 16 in urban areas; in Prince Edward Island, 15; and in Newfoundland, 15.
We feel, therefore, the program should act as an incentive to children to pursue their educational opportunities even though they are not legally required to do so by provincial laws. As was stated by my colleague the Minister of Finance in his budget speech of March 16 last, the government believes that the expenditure involved will be an important investment in raising the level of skills and ability of our labour force, and thus will improve the growth and development of our economy. This measure is one we can afford this year. It will help young Canadians to fit themselves for better jobs.
We are hopeful, Mr. Speaker, that the allowances can become effective with the beginning of the next school year in September. It will be necessary, of course, to forward application forms to parents throughout the summer. Hon. members will realize this is not an automatic payment, but there must be an application to have the children qualify under the act. We are prepared to send out these application forms and set the machinery in motion as soon as parliament will have approved the legislation. Since all hon. members have heretofore indicated their approval in principle, it is hoped that there remains ample time for a thorough discussion of the details of the bill. I therefore respectfully move the adoption of this bill to provide additional allowances for young children.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have urged for some considerable time that a measure such as is now before us, in one form or another, should be presented to parliament. Therefore we welcome this legislation, and we hope it

will not take very long for parliament to deal with it so the application forms might be sent out, and so the payments to be made under this legislation to the parents of 16 and 17 year old children might be in their hands commencing in September of this year.
All of us in the house agreed readily to the proposal that there be no debate at the resolution stage of this measure. I think there is also a general disposition today to proceed as expeditiously as we can with this stage of this legislation. As I say, we have been asking for it ourselves for a long time, and we support the measure now that it has been placed before us.
However, one or two issues do arise. One of them has already been stated by the hon. member for Middlesex West. He has stated his opposition to this measure for the reasons that he holds. He has stated that opposition quite clearly. I must say that I do not agree with the criticism he has made of the form in which this legislation is presented to us. I know, Mr. Speaker, it would be very nice, neat and tidy if all legislation in this country could be drafted in such a way, for all time, that it would be uniform in its application across Canada. But that is not the Canada in which we live.
The hon. member for Middlesex West said we should extend our efforts to hold this land together in unity. I agree with him. However, this does not necessarily mean that we achieve unity by establishing some rigid mould which we insist must be applied across the country. It sems to me we have to take cognizance of the different approaches, the different scales of values that there are in the various parts of our country. It seems to me that this legislation does that. The fact is, and I have had occasion to say this with regard to other pieces of legislation, that the people of Quebec value their autonomy in a very special way. Equally it is a fact that the Canadians of the other nine provinces place a special value on the benefits of confederation, place a special value on what comes from the central government. Although it may be a lot more difficult to work things out in the light of these two facts, I think if we are going to be realistic, if we are going to hold this land together in unity, we have to accept these two facts.
What I see in this legislation is an effort to meet these facts; an effort to recognize that Canadians in nine of our provinces like receiving payments such as these from the central government, but that it is also a fact that the Canadians in one province

like to feel they are getting them through their own provincial government. I see nothing wrong in accommodating this legislation to the facts of Canadian life. I think we are going to have to do more of this kind of thing. If we do it carefully, if we do it with a realization of the values of our people in the various parts of the country, I think instead of causing a division in Canada it could help strengthen that unity that we value so greatly.
I do not criticize the hon. member for Middlesex West for raising the point he did this afternoon. I think it is well that this point should be raised, that criticism such as he made should be stated quite clearly. I think it is a good idea also for all of us to look at the issue clearly and realize the kind of pattern we are going to have to develop if we are to hold this land together in unity. I suggest if we start developing a pattern whereby we do achieve a situation that recognizes for the people of nine provinces their emphasis upon the values of confederation, their desire to receive things from the central government, and recognizes the desire of the people in the other province for the autonomy that means so much to them, instead of causing disunity it could actually bring about unity.
I suspect it has taken a great deal of soulsearching, a great deal of negotiating, a great deal of very difficult drafting to come forward with this legislation in this form. It occurs to me that a good job has been done. We do not have the kind of reservations about it that were expressed by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas). We shall support the bill.
I am also glad, having in mind the suggestion that it is good to say things openly, that it has been said quite clearly by the minister that this legislation in the main has as its aim inducing parents to persuade their 16 and 17 year old children to stay in school. I am glad she made it clear that it does have an educational motive at its base. This is something we are sometimes reluctant to talk about in public because of the fact that education in itself is an exclusive provincial responsibility under the British North America Act.
In many respects we have already gone into this field. We have devised vocational education grants, university grants, and Canada Council grants in ways that use federal money to assist in raising the level of education in Canada without interfering with the provincial responsibility for education as such.
Youth Allowances
I think we should go on doing that kind of thing. That is precisely one of the things this piece of legislation does. It helps to raise the level of education by encouraging more parents to encourage their children to stay in school, yet it does not interfere in any way, shape or form with provincial control over education as such. Therefore I am glad that the legislation in its drafting is geared to the educational question, and I am glad the minister stated that quite clearly in her speech this afternoon.
I note with interest that the legislation has been drafted so that it is possible for a 16 or 17 year old to draw the allowance for the full 12 months provided he is in school up until April, and again in school by October. I also notice the inducements that some of the details seem to provide to encourage a student to continue in school for a second year. All told, the people who have done this drafting have wrestled with a difficult problem and have come up with a very satisfactory answer.
We in common with members in all parties in the house, have for a long time been looking for family allowances, or youth allowances, to be extended to keep children in school when they are 16 and 17 years old. We are only sorry it has taken so long, but now that the legislation is before us we support it, and we hope it can get through all its stages in this day's sitting.

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
If the house will allow me to reply to what was said by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) perhaps I could clear up one or two misunderstandings. It has been suggested that there will be differences in the payments in different parts of the country, and this is one of the things that has been cleared up.
Hon. members will recall that when the proposal to extend youth allowances to the 16 and 17 year old age group was first considered we were confronted with four complicating factors. These were some of the things we had in mind at the time the income tax resolution was being debated in the house, when I made the remarks quoted by the hon. member.
Those complicating factors were, first, that in one province, the province of Quebec, that province had been paying school allowances to the parents of 16 and 17 year olds for some years. Second, these payments in the province of Quebec were at the rate of $10 per month for ten months of the year only.

Youth Allowances
The proposed payments by the federal government were to be at the rate of $10 per month for 12 months. Third, under the Quebec plan payments were not made on account of disabled children age 16 and 17. Under the federal plan it was proposed that the payments would apply both to children who remain in school and to those who are unable to do so because of disability.
Fourth, the personal exemptions under the federal Income Tax Act are reduced from $550 to $300 per annum in the case of children whose parents are entitled to benefits under the Family Allowances Act, but this differential is not applied in the case of 16 and 17 year olds entitled to school allowances in the province of Quebec.
Those were four complicating factors, and because of them it was originally proposed to pay to the government of Quebec an annual sum equal to the net amount which parents of children in Quebec would have received if the payments to them were made by the federal government direct, less the additional amounts of income taxes they would pay because of the reduction in the exemption from $550 to $300 per annum. In addition, some adjustment would be necessary due to the fact that parents in Quebec would receive $10 a month for ten months only and would not receive anything on account of disabled children.
In the course of that debate on the income tax resolution the hon. member for Middlesex West, and others, pointed out that under this formula cases could arise where the federal income tax payable by a parent living on one side of the Ottawa river, for example, would be different from the tax payable by a parent in exactly similar circumstances residing on the other side of the river. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) asked me questions, and as a result of his questions this became quite clear to all hon. members of the house. I may say this difficulty was pointed out by members on all sides of the house.
Since that debate in April the government has given further consideration to the best way of handling this difficult and complex situation, and in the meantime certain things have happened. In the first place the province of Quebec enacted legislation extending its $10 a month school allowance to a full 12 months. Second, Quebec has now introduced a bill which, if it is passed by the Quebec legislature, will provide that the same amounts are paid to disabled children in that province, so that as far as the payments are

concerned they will be the same in all parts of Canada.
I am sure we were all very pleased about this development because I know all of us share the feeling of the hon. member for Middlesex West that it would be too bad if, in an important social measure of this kind, there were differences between the benefits in different parts of Canada. In the light of these changed circumstances it seems all the more important that people all over Canada should be treated in exactly the same way.
Accordingly it is proposed that there should be no reduction in the exemptions from $550 to $300 per annum in respect of children aged 16 and 17 whose parents receive youth allowances. There is good justification for this of course, quite apart from the desirability of having a uniform system across the country, because it costs more to keep 16 and 17 year olds at school than it does to look after dependant children of younger ages. I think most of the parents in the house would agree with me that 16 and 17 are the critical years for many young people when they decide whether to drop out of school or to continue further education.
The extra $250 of income tax exemption for their parents will place an additional emphasis on the goal which I think is shared by members of all parties in the house, which is to create conditions under which young people are more likely to stay in school longer and thus receive the training which will fit them for the kind of jobs likely to be available in the future. For this reason I think there is ample justification for adopting a different approach in the case of youth allowances for 16 and 17 year olds from that followed in the case of family allowances.
I appreciate being allowed to make this interjection at this time. It seemed important to clear up the points which had been raised by hon. members opposite and which, I had a feeling, might be raised by others if an explanation were not given.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
The Social Credit party is on record since its national convention in 1961 as being in favour of extending family allowances to 16 and 17 year old children. The proposal before us this afternoon is slightly different but I do not believe it is so different as to warrant our taking any exception to it.
We are pleased to note that the bill provides for allowances to be made in the amount of $10 per month in respect of students attending school, as well as for those who are incapacitated either mentally or physically to

the extent that they are unable to attend school. We know there have been many attempts made during the past few years to improve the educational standards of the young people in Canada. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on the retraining of older workers who have been displaced by automation in one form or another. We therefore feel it is essential that an effort be made to improve educational standards and that incentives should be offered in this regard. We are pleased to consider this measure as another step forward in the improvement of the educational standards of this country.
We have noted over the years with some concern that a revolution is taking place in the industrial life in this country as a result of automation. This is affecting not only young people who are entering the work force but also people who have been engaged in what they thought was a steady job for years. There is growing apprehension about the permanency of even certain occupations which have been reasonably stable for a long time. Only a few days ago a memorandum was sent to the President of the United States concerning this important matter. I am bringing it to the attention of the house this afternoon because I believe many of us have failed to appreciate the implications of this revolution brought about by automation and have done none of the thinking which needs to be done in order to change some of our basic concepts about the relationship between jobs and income. This memorandum which was sent to the President of the United States was signed by 23 eminent personalities in the United States including economists and university professors. I do not wish to spend a great deal of time on it, but I would like to draw the following to the attention of the house:
President Johnson was asked Sunday to consider "radically new strategies to meet radically new circumstances" in the nation's economic and social life as a result of automation and technological change.
A 723-page memorandum called The Triple Revolution was sent to the President by a group of 26 economists, labour leaders, authors and educators who said it was prepared "out of a feeling of foreboding for the nation's future".
I intend to read just one more paragraph; I shall summarize this greatly:
They proposed some form of paying everyone so they can buy the unbelievable quantity of goods the country can produce, even though everyone doesn't work to earn their incomes. There just won't be enough jobs to permit everyone to work, they argued.

I am not prepared at this stage to go as far as to say we can enter upon an economic order in which everyone will be paid an income whether or not they work, but I do believe we have come far enough to recognize that most of the unemployment in Canada today occurs among those with the least education-the least amount of training and skill. As long as this is the situation I think the subject before us this afternoon is an extremely important one. The memorandum to which I have referred goes on to say:
As jobs diminish proportionate to the work force some way must be found to permit the growing population to get a fair share of the abundant economy.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) has pointed out that there is at the present time a compulsory requirement that children attend school until a certain age. This is a provincial matter, of course, and in some provinces the age is 14 years. In others it is 15 years, and in two provinces I think it is as high as 16 years. In this day and age, taking into account the skills which are required in certain jobs, it is impossible for a young person to obtain by the age of 16 the skills needed to cope with the social and economic order which exists today and I suggest the provinces should consider increasing the age up to which attendance in schools is compulsorily required from 14 or 15 or 16, to perhaps 18. This would not impose any hardship on the vast majority of the children of this country because most parents, even today, although they are not required to do so, send their children to school until they are 18 or even older. I think the tremendous expenditures we undertake in this country in providing welfare, relief and unemployment benefits each year would be greatly reduced if the standards of education and training could be improved. For this reason I think the incentive provided by these youth allowances is to be welcomed. Perhaps it does not go far enough, but having said this I must add that it is perhaps as far as the federal government can go. At least it is a step in the right direction.
A few minutes ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) said that people all over Canada should be treated in the same way. Mr. Speaker, the government is to be commended for introducing Bill No. C-108. In extending youth allowances by two years, thousands of girls and boys will be enabled to complete high school and thus reduce the percentage of student dropouts in this country. This is the most compelling justification for the bill, as the minister pointed out earlier this afternoon in her statement.
An inevitable result will be to increase university enrolment in every Canadian prov-

Youth Allowances
ince. For this and other reasons the number ol students attending institutions of higher learning is expected to double in the next ten years. To meet this problem federal authorities have a responsibility to support provincial governments in all ways consistent with our constitution. The pressing need of the immediate future will be to develop a systematic long range program for the planning and financing of university development with respect both to operating costs and capital requirements for the years ahead.
The goal of such a plan must be to enable universities in all parts of the country to discharge their responsibilities in a way that does not place any one institution at an advantage over another with respect to the payment of staff or the provision of facilities. In providing strong leadership of this kind, the federal government would make a contribution to national unity that could not be achieved in any other way. A commendable beginning has been made voluntarily by the Canadian universities foundation. They have established a commission on the financing of higher education at a cost of $200,000. The money has been contributed by the Ford foundation and by Canadian industries.
Their report, which is expected in 1965 will include:
(a)	Prospective financial requirements of universities and colleges for operation, research, physical facilities and student aid;
(b)	The proportion of the financial support of higher education which should be provided by tuition fees, contributions from governments, corporations, foundations and individuals;
(c)	Policies regarding, the allocation of funds for higher education and criteria by which institutions and students should be deemed eligible to receive such aid;
(d)	Organization for the financing of higher education, including the role of appropriate agencies for the distribution of funds.
This voluntary effort should mark the beginning of a continuing task to be undertaken by a government agency similar to that of the scientific secretariat recently announced in the House of Commons by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). The time has come for a bold and imaginative approach in developing a policy of assisting the provinces to provide adequate facilities for the higher education of their young people. Effective leadership must begin from a centre of study and planning established by some responsible federal agency.

I wish to give briefly five reasons to justify federal involvement in higher education as well as in research.
(1)	The Canadian union of students maintain that only one half of the young people who are capable of higher education ever enrol in a Canadian university. They assert that such a waste of human talent is indefensible. Since every democratic state desires to see its people achieve the full extent of their potential development, a federal government in concert with provincial authorities must accept a large share of responsibility for improving this condition.
(2)	The work of universities does not end at the provincial boundaries. In each of the larger universities there are students from all the provinces. Likewise the graduates of the universities are distributed over the entire country. They are one of the most mobile elements in the working population and comprise a source of skilled and educated personnel which is available to the nation as a whole. Since all benefit from the work of our most capable men and women, it is not unreasonable to ask that all should contribute to their training.
(3)	In our increasingly complex industrial life, the role of the universities in sustaining and improving society is now vital. Never before has the public welfare in its social, cultural and economic aspects been so dependant upon the effective functioning of our universities. This calls for a high level of investment in higher education both from private industry and from provincial and federal governments.
(4)	The commission on Canada's economic prospects, of which the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) was chairman, expressed the following view in 1956:
It is our duty to point out most emphatically that it is vitally important to Canada's future for the status of our universities to be improved and strengthened and for their facilities to be increased. In this connection it must suffice us to express the strong opinion that no government which bears any share of responsibility for the future economic development of this country can allow a solution to the pressing financial problems of the universities to go by default.
(5)	The federal government has recognized that it has a responsibility for supporting the universities by its per capita grants to the provinces, by its grants to scholars through the national research council, by capital grants through Canada Council, and by loans for student residences through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

While these contributions have been praiseworthy in the past, they are already inadequate today. There is little evidence that there is any appreciation of the tremendous needs of the future in all parts of Canada. One fact is clear: Only the federal government has the resources to provide the certainty and uniformity essential to any broad scheme of financial assistance to higher education in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have carefully considered this Bill No. C-108 derived from the Family Allowances Act of 1944-45.
Personally, I support this measure and I will vote for it, but I should like to make a few reserves and suggestions with respect to its constitutionality. In the light of the Canadian constitution, the fields of social security and education are a responsibility of the provinces and normally should be administered by the provinces. Besides, on the occasion of a number of federal-provincial conferences, namely those of 1963 and 1964, as well as previous conferences, the province of Quebec and other provinces clearly expressed their views on this matter.
Mr. Speaker, the fact that a fiscal compensation would be granted to the province of Quebec indicates that the federal government admits the unconstitutionality of its legislation. It makes the payment of school allowances conditional, as it imposes conditions on the provinces which have the full responsibility in the field of education.
I know that there have been for some time exchanges between the officials of the federal government and those of some provinces, especially the province of Quebec.
The government should hand over to the provinces a wider taxation field and enable them to adequately discharge their responsibilities in fields like social security and education.
This Bill No. C-108, Mr. Speaker, is in some way similar to the Family Allowances Act of 1944-45 and two other pieces of social security legislation, the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Old Age Pensions Act.
In 1940 administrative responsibility for unemployment insurance was given to the federal government, but, in order to meet the requirements and respect the rights of the provinces, the constitution was amended and the federal government was able to set up a fund to provide for unemployment insurance benefits. Moreover, as regards old age pensions, a constitutional amendment was passed
Youth Allowances
in 1951 to enable the federal government to legislate and to establish an old age security fund.
When the federal government passed the Family Allowances Act, in 1944, it ignored the provinces and did not amend the constitution. It did not set up a special fund but merely drew upon the consolidated revenue fund.
That is why I suggest that the government should propose an amendment to the constitution to legalize its action even though I feel that social, educational, civil and family matters come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that social security and education should receive special consideration at the next federal-provincial conference, in order that an agreement might be arrived at in those fields, if possible, and that their taxation fields might be returned to the provinces so that they might be able to fully exercise their prerogatives.
Mr. Speaker, it is well known that for over 25 years conflicts have arisen between the provinces and the federal government concerning their respective responsibilities, in order to know whether the federal government should intervene in those fields which, normally, come under provincial jurisdiction. On the other hand, the provinces endeavour to recuperate their taxation powers as much as possible so that the objectives of the federal government might not come into conflict with their rights.
Consequently, it is my opinion that serious consideration should be given to social security and education during a forthcoming federal-provincial conference, in order that these fields may come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces with the federal government returning to the provinces the necessary taxation fields which would enable them to discharge their responsibilities. By so doing, I feel that there would be less frustration and that confederation would be strengthened.

Most hon. members approve of it on the basis that it will assist parents to keep their children in school for another two years, but there is one small criticism I have to offer. It will only assist parents to keep children in school during the years 16 and 17, and a little elementary arithmetic will indicate that most of the children who leave school at age 17 will not have completed grade 12, let alone grade 13 in Ontario. In some instances this might cause a bit a difficulty for the parents and therefore I regret that the assistance is not being made available also for those aged 18 years.
Mention has been made that the program will cost us some $27 million this year, plus the amount that will be given to the province of Quebec as a direct grant. This is quite a bit of money, but from my standpoint it is a justifiable expenditure. It is a certainty that no country ever suffers from having a highly educated population and anything we can do to assist in raising the general level of education is to be highly commended. For this reason it is a good thing that this allowance is being granted to 16 and 17 year olds and I am only sorry that the 18 year olds are not included.
We know unemployment is always greatest in those areas where the people are the most

poorly educated. Of course there are exceptions to every rule, but this is the general experience, and if this is so again we have a very good reason for making this grant to parents.
I am also glad that the province of Quebec has seen fit to co-operate in this particular case. In some other instances there has been a great deal of difficulty in securing co-operation from that province but, as was pointed out by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) this afternoon, by modifying their legislation they have gone along with this plan. I hope it will soon come out of the limbo of the unknown, wherever it is, and be presented to us at an early date.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to make a few remarks on Bill No. C-108 now before us.
I very much approve of a legislation providing an allowance for our young people, not because it is particularly generous, but because it recognizes a principle which we, in this corner of the house, have advocated for a long time. Thus, the government admits the necessity and urgency of enabling our young people to attend school where they will get the necessary education to get on in life.

Yet, we have to realize that this legislation is but a faltering step towards education. The old line political parties have accustomed us to expect a somewhat reluctant step by step advance with regard to social legislation, though, of course, when there was a question of taxing the Canadian people they came running forth with giant steps. Yet, it must be admitted that this piece of legislation will make things easier for the young people and their parents who have to provide for their children, and it will increase opportunities for education.
However, as everybody knows and as several members stated tonight in this house, Canadians expect much more from the government with regard to the education of our young people. Today, when for the past ten years at least, we have been through a period of unemployment on a more or less catastrophical scale, our industries can clearly get along without our young people, thus enabling them to get a more thorough education according to their capacities and wishes in order to help them face a rapidly setting in automation. In this country, under our system, machinery is gradually playing a more important role and therefore employees, workers, the people operating those machines will have to have wider knowledge and increased ability in order to make them as efficient as possible and control them instead of being controlled by them.
This legislation to assist young people may make this a little easier, and that is what we want. However, we, on this side of the house-and I have personally asked for it time and time again-would have rather liked a more generous legislation enabling the parents to keep their children longer in school without depriving the other children in the family.
Considering the cost of education today and what it will be tomorrow, it is obvious that $10 a month is far from being enough; but I hope that this first step will enable the government to realize, through experience, that families need more money. This assistance to students, which I will call a salary, should be given as long as they are continuing their studies and should not stop at 18 years of age, as now provided by the act. We know that young people have to go to school longer than that to obtain the necessary education to face life's responsibilities.
Therefore, I would ask the government to consider the possibility of paying this salary as long as our young boys and girls are

I

hope the minister is making a note of this particular point.
I know there have been difficulties in the past with regard to institutions accumulating these funds, placing them in deposit accounts and drawing the interest. This was a practice that existed in the past, and I hope it has been discontinued in so far as the earning of interest is concerned, because this money does not belong to the institution or the substitute parent. I do not want to discuss a particular clause, but there seems to be an exemption for the institution as defined in the regulation. With that reservation or that question, I will await the minister's explanation.

With respect to the question posed by my honourable predecessor, and others, as to the number of individuals who might be required to administer this legislation, it was suggested that a whole new staff would be required, but the existing division of family allowances and old age security is expected to administer the program through its 10 regional offices. speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
My hon. friend and other hon. members have suggested amendments to the Family Allowances Act, but I would draw to the attention of the committee that there are a number of substantial differences between the matters dealt with by the family allowances legislation and this legislation. It should be borne in mind that the family allowances legislation is available to every child resident in Canada up to age 16. This is not the case with youth allowances. These are available to a restricted group of people, many of whom are not compulsorily required to attend school. As I have pointed out the school leaving ages are 14, 15 and 16 years

for the various provinces. Furthermore, a number of these people are already employed and do not qualify.
In addition we have dealt in this legislation with the payment of allowances for the summer months. If members of the committee will think about the problem for a few minutes they will realize there is considerably more involved than the matter of paying family allowances by simply continuing those allowances to the higher age groups. Schools, at least in the provinces with which I am familiar, normally operate until some time in the month of June. Universities may close in April or May. In other provinces other months are occupied. This is legislation which we hope, through the 10 regional offices, will be operated in an identical way regardless of what the school year may be. Remember that under the regulations schools and universities will encompass very different kinds of institutions.
Therefore in order to satisfy the Auditor General that parliament's wishes are met in the way the legislation is administered, it will be necessary to delay the payment of summer benefits until the fall when it is established that the young persons have returned to school, and at that stage they will catch up with the summer payments. In some cases with those who leave early in the spring, payments will continue, provided it is not the year in which they are expected to graduate.
Earlier my hon. friend suggested that family allowances were universal in application except for the restriction of the residential qualification. This is true, but rather an important qualification; and then of course there is the condition that the child stays on in school. But the two types of legislation, family allowances and youth allowances, are different in purpose to some degree, and very different, in application. However it will be noticed by members of the committee that in drawing the legislation the draftsmen have tried-with the experience of family allowances, which is now 13 or 14 years old-to adopt the phraseology, and benefit from the experience which has already been obtained under family allowances legislation.
It will be noted that we are able to provide for an individual who applies late, possibly because he or she has not heard about these benefits. They can obtain back payments for a period. That is not permitted under the legislation governing family allowances as it

now stands. We have gone further here because we believe it might well be possible that individual parents would not be aware they were entitled to these benefits, and we feel they should not lose them in the circumstances.
Perhaps I could answer on clause 1 some of the other questions which have been asked. The hon. member for Ontario suggested there was a gap existing under this legislation and that students were not covered between the time they left grade 12 and the time they entered university, at which time it is expected that they, the students, will be able to apply for and obtain university loans under forthcoming legislation. In my opinion the hon. member is speaking of Ontario when he talks about grades 12 and 13. It should be borne in mind that in many provinces a child is 17 when he or she completes the first year in university. So in fact there is no gap. This is simply an age limit. It has no reference to attendance at a university or a school.

The two hon. members who have just spoken have been discussing the differences between education systems in the various provinces. It is for this very reason that an age cut-off date has been chosen. The bill does not propose taking any child to a specific level of education, only to a specific age, namely the eighteenth birthday.
With respect to the point raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West, the legislation indicates that the parent who maintains a child-perhaps I should say the individual who receives the amount-shall include, as far as the bill is concerned, an agency or corporate body such as a child placing agency or children's aid society. However the regulations will exclude the institutions themselves. In other words, if a child is maintained by an institution the institution will not be in receipt of these allowances, but if a child is placed in an institution and maintained by an agency or an actual person the allowance will be paid. I am informed that the definition in the regulations will be:
An orphanage, a children's home, a shelter, refuge or other building, not being a private residence

Youth Allowances
or building, in which children are cared for apart from their parents.
Those are the institutions which will be excluded.
As to the situation in colleges militaires, I am informed that such colleges will not be excepted. They will be included in the definition as schools or universities, so any child in a college which falls into this category will have the benefit of the allowance if maintained by the parents, not if maintained by the state.

Mr. Chairman, hon. members will be interested in the type of thing that has to be done in the time left between the passage of this legislation and the making of the first payment. All this of course is conditional upon passage by both houses, and royal assent. In addition to regulations having been drafted, a notice has been prepared which, subject to the passage of this legislation by parliament, will be mailed out to all parents who have children who will qualify either in August or September in particular. The names of these individuals come to us from our family allowance records, and hon. members will realize that we will have the lists of those moving into this age bracket. This is a bilingual notice and it will be sent out to all such parents. It will give the details of this program. This notice, or letter, will be mailed with the August cheques. In addition there will be sent a bilingual application form which any parent who believes that his or her child qualifies under the definitions in the act will be asked to complete and return. There will be enclosed a self-addressed envelope which will be addressed to the nearest regional director, in which the completed application should be enclosed. That will be done in August, presupposing the passage of this legislation and royal assent.
This will enable payments to begin in the month of September. When I told the committee that 12 months are being allowed to pick up past payments which are due, I meant that this will be done without fetters of any kind. If individuals are absent from
Youth Allowances
the country or have not heard of the legislation, they will be able to go to August of 1965, make their application, and still collect the payment for 12 months back, for each month that the child qualifies. Therefore if someone misses noticing this legislation in August-though this is hardly likely, because they will receive their cheque and read about this legislation then-and does not apply, for instance in September, October or November, the child will lose no benefit whatsoever, provided the parent or individual who maintains the child makes application at a subsequent time. In that event we will date the payments back to the date on which the child qualified; that is to say, up to September 1, 1964. Therefore the child should not in any way lose any benefit.
Although this is a new and rather complicated piece of legislation in that it is selective in its application to those who may qualify, we have allowed 12 months to catch up on any tag ends or on anyone who may not have heard of the legislation.
