speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a question in relation to clause 2 (h), which says:
''province providing schooling allowances" means a province prescribed by a regulation made on the recommendation of the minister for the purposes of this act as a province in which provision is made, pursuant to any law of the province enacted before the coming into force of this act-
Does this mean that while at the moment these particular arrangements can be made with the province of Quebec, any other province is excluded in the future from handling the thing in the same way?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. I think it is clear from this legislation that it is open to any province up until the time that royal assent is given to this legislation to enact similar legislation. At the moment I know of only one province with similar legislation. While we have no indication that this is likely to happen in any other province, it cannot happen after royal assent is given to this legislation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: In other words, the principle of opting out shall not apply to this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, paragraph (d)
says:
"maintain" means maintains wholly or substantially and "substantially" has such meaning as may be prescribed;
Could the minister inform this committee what is meant by " 'substantially' has such meaning as may be prescribed"? I understand that this will be written into the regulations, but can she inform the committee what is the thinking of the department at this time with regard to the use of the word "substantially"?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
Draft regulations have been prepared and are similar to the family allowance regulations. A parent maintains a dependant youth substantially if the value of the contribution made by the parent in cash or otherwise for the care, maintenance, education or advancement of the youth is $5 or more per month exclusive of the allowance and such value exceeds the value of the

Youth Allowances
contribution for such purpose made by any other person who has applied for the allowance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: There is another question with regard to paragraph (h) of clause 2. Would the minister agree that paragraph (h) provides a special privilege for the province of Quebec for all time to come?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Only perhaps if no other province takes advantage of it. I do not think it is a special privilege since identical provisions are available to all children of the same age and the same attendance at school anywhere in Canada. I am of the opinion that members of the committee generally are concerned with the benefit which is passed on to our youth and not with such technical matters. It happens that the province of Quebec is the only province that has brought in such legislation. I understand its legislation has been in effect since 1961. It might very well have been any other province and it might well be that the territories or some other province might call together a special meeting of their legislature and enact such legislation. If so, that province will then qualify, of course.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if she does not think that the principle she has just enunciated should apply to other acts that her department administers as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: We are only dealing in the welfare field at the moment with this particular piece of legislation. However, I have some idea of what my hon. friend is referring to.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: I have a question for the minister. I had an inquiry from the parents of a retarded youth who is 17 years of age and is in a school for retarded children. Will the allowance be paid in such cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: If the child is maintained by its parent the allowance will be paid.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Will it continue to be paid when the boy reaches 18 years of age or will the allowance stop when he reaches his 18th birthday, as the minister said a few minutes ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
As I pointed out on second reading, this allowance stops at age 18 regardless of whether the child would otherwise qualify, but a retarded or disabled child would then be able to apply through the provincial authorities under the shared cost program for a disabled person's allowance which, as the

hon. member knows, is considerably larger than $10 per month.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, under paragraph (i) of clause 2 school or university is defined. What will be the situation with regard to students taking business courses, typing and so on, after they have finished grade 10, let us say, in business schools where such courses are provided? Are such institutions included under the definition in paragraph (i>?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the child is in full-time attendance at such a school which will upgrade skills, payment will then be made to the parent. It may be that members of the committee might wish to know the proposed method of dealing with this. The regulations as presently contemplated will exclude by defining "excepted educational institutions" and will not try to include everything in a long list. The suggested phraseology is to this effect: "Excepted educational institution" referred to in paragraph (i) of section 2 of the act means a school, university or educational institution that does not provide training or instruction of an educational, vocational or technical nature to improve the qualifications of dependant youth for employment or a career or for carrying on or engaging in a trade, business, profession or occupation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister about the definition of the word "parent". As I understand the situation, under the Family Allowances Act the parent is the mother of the child unless there is some reason for payment to the father. Is the definition of "parent" included in this legislation intended to bring about the same result?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. It is intended that the cheque will be payable to the mother. As a lawyer my hon. friend knows that there are many cases where payment is not made to the mother but to an alternative parent, and exactly the same procedure will be followed under this legislation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: I have a question I should like to ask the minister. I am not sure whether her answer covered the question asked by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale. With regard to students taking courses at private schools and institutions where they learn certain technical skills such as typing, office routine and so on, is it the intention of the minister to include business colleges of that type under the definition of "school"?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Yes. I read the proposed legislation and they are included. The criterion is that attendance be full-time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: As long as they are attending full-time?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think that full-time students only are eligible for family allowances. However, there are many Canadian students in the various provinces attending night classes and taking four years to complete their studies instead of two or three. If those students are attending evening classes it is because, obviously, they cannot afford to follow the regular day course.
Now, when schools or universities giving such evening courses are recognized by the provinces, I wonder if the act could not be amended so as to permit such students to receive family allowances. That would surely encourage students who cannot afford to follow the regular day course to continue and complete their studies. Should the minister take such steps, I believe she would indirectly help such students to improve their education.
I also wonder what amount of money the Canadian government would have to spend annually for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I pointed out in my remarks on second reading, this legislation is not to cover employed children in the two years with which we are concerned. The purpose is to enable children to stay in school or to go back to school if they have left. My hon. friend is dealing with a young person who is employed during the day and goes to night school and such a person will not qualify. Night schools are not included. This covers full-time attendance in lieu of employment. It is anticipated that the young adults to whom he refers would have to have recourse to legislation already enacted by the Department of Labour.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: I have a question on this clause. I am assuming that subclause 2(a) means when a person ceases to be a parent as defined by the act and this simply means if they move to Quebec?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: If they move to Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: Then, subclause 3, can the minister give a brief explanation as to how she expects this responsibility to reflect on the parent in notifying when the allowance ceases to be payable?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT BETWEEN AGES OF 16 AND 18
speechtext: As will be seen in subclause 3 the parent must advise us, so obviously a deceased parent cannot do so. I am informed, however, that we have recourse to the Vital Statistics Act for those who die and such information is checked in the normal manner with regard to family allowances. The same checking procedure would take place. It is anticipated also that on the reverse side of the cheque will appear a warning to the parent, together with a certification where the signature is to be placed for endorsement of the cheque, that the child qualifies. This declaration will, month by month, bring to the attention of the parents that it is an offence to make a false declaration. It may very well be that there will be some few individuals who will be caught in the normal checking procedure, as there are in connection with old age allowances and

Youth Allowances
all other allowances with which my friend had several years experience.
However everything is being done under the regulations and within the act in order to prevent most unfortunate circumstances where, by error, a parent who is no longer qualified continues to receive and cash cheques, and then subsequently the department could come along and ask for repayment.
That is all I am concerned about.
Then, I take it that clause 5(b) means that the dependant who graduates from high school at 17 years and 8 months will then stop drawing allowance, is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, the hon. member is correct, or the child might die or move outside the country or his parents may move outside the country. If the child, let us say, is physically or mentally handicapped, but is suddenly cured and does not go to school or university, he would no longer qualify.
If three months later he goes to a university, what happens then?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Provided he has not
reached his 18th birthday, he reapplies and is reinstated.
He would not then get any allowance for the three months between the time he graduates from grade 12 and the time he starts university.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If this were a break between courses and not an unnatural break then he would be paid for the intervening months. If for instance he stopped in the middle of a year, went to work for a couple of months and then came back, it will be appreciated by members of the committee he would not be reimbursed for the months in which he, himself, broke his education.

That is not the situation I had in mind. Most of these children would have to wait until they got the results of their grade 12 examinations before they could be sure they would be attending university. There would be no break in their minds, but there may be some question as to whether they were or were not qualified to collect the $10 per month.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
As was pointed out, we have borne this in mind and clause 6 deals with it specifically. The child cannot lose because

he can apply for and receive retroactive payments at any time up to a year.

I have one other comment to make. Members from Ontario have pointed out that children attending grade 13 would not graduate at age 18 and would be unable to continue drawing this allowance. I think it should be understood that there are no provinces in Canada where the average student would graduate at age 17. As I pointed out earlier this evening this can be verified by a little simple arithmetic. Most children start school at age 6 and they go into grade 1 at age 7. If you add 12 grades to age 6, you will find that in grade 12 a student will be 18 years of age. I believe it would cost very little extra money if we were to continue the policy that has been applied so as to stop paying the allowance once the student graduates. The total cost would not be increased by 50 per cent. The increase would be comparatively small-I should not say "comparatively small", but it would not be the 50 per cent which might appear to be at first glance.

My question is based on subclause (1) of clause 5 as it is read in conjunction with clause 12. I should like to ask the minister if she really has any hope whatever of enforcing subclause (1) of clause 5 which provides that the allowance payable to the parent shall be applied exclusively for the care, education or advancement of the child. I can see where there may be some cases in which parents receive allowances and do not use them in the proper manner for the maintenance of the child. I can see where there may be a situation in which the department might want to suspend the allowance or even go so far as to prosecute the parent.
In looking at clause 12, however, which is the penalty section, I find there is no penalty provided for a situation of this kind. Subclause (1) of clause 5 therefore seems to me to be an absolutely useless clause. It is a declaration of intention but it is not enforceable in any way. I wonder what real advantage there is in having it there?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, this was one of the things that bothered me when I first saw the draft legislation. It will be appreciated that this is an identical provision to that which is in the Family Allowances Act. There has been a wealth of experience in this matter in which it is found there is a miniscule amount which is diverted away from benefit of the child.
It would be extremely rare if in fact a prosecution were contemplated at all. If I

may make a personal remark to my hon. friend, there is no doubt this is the reason the amounts are paid to the mother because she would have somewhat more interest in applying the payments for the care and education of the children. Experience has been extremely good with the Family Allowances Act. Canadians appreciate the purpose of this legislation and act within the law accordingly.

Is there anything in the remaining clauses or regulations which would permit the department to take any action whatever, if it found this was not being followed? Can the allowance be suspended in a case where the parent is not using the money for the purpose intended?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes. It is not contemplated there would be a prosecution, but the same kind of practice would be followed as in family allowances, that is, an alternative payee would be named so that a responsible person would see that the money went for the care and education of the child.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare

Youth Allowances

Youth Allowances

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION TOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION TOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the revision of certain fiscal arrangements with the provinces and to provide adjustments of fiscal arrangements and taxation provisions consequential upon the provision of youth allowances to parents resident in certain provinces.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION TOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
No one should be misled by the apparently simple wording of the resolution. This is a very complicated matter and I think it might be helpful if I were to make a fairly extended explanation of what is proposed, as the bill, if the resolution passes, will cover a number of subjects and I should like to be certain that all members of the committee appreciate its complexities.
In the past year or so the amount of federal-provincial consultation has been increased very considerably. I think it is fair to say that the federal government has demonstrated its willingness to deal in a practical way with some of the urgent financial problems of the provinces.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION TOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Cut out the politics, Walter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION TOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I had to have some sort of introduction.
We have had two federal-provincial conferences which have dealt with a range of matters including the important question of tax-sharing and there have been a number of other conferences which have dealt with specific subjects such as the municipal development and loan fund and the Canada pension plan. As a result of these consultations and our consideration of the financial problems of the provinces the government has come to the conclusion that the fiscal relationship with the provinces was in need of modification before the expiry of the present arrangements on March 31, 1967. Accordingly we made certain proposals to the
Dominion-Provincial Relations provinces at the conclusion of the conference which was held on November 26-27 1963 and again following the conclusion of the conference in Quebec city held from March 31 to April 2, 1964. These proposals will be dealt with in the bill which will be presented in due course.
The fiscal proposals presented to the federal-provincial conference last November involved a change in the basis of equalization and also an increase in the share of the estate tax for the provinces, both to take effect for the fiscal year 1964-65. I think I might read two or three paragraphs from the statement which was issued by the Prime Minister at the conclusion of that conference because they summarize what was agreed to there as concisely as I think could be done. I quote:
On balance, therefore, we have concluded that the most acceptable solution is to restore the basis of equalization which was established in 1956 but subsequently altered. That is to say, equalization will be paid up to the average yield of the standard taxes in the top two provinces.
The other main point under discussion yesterday was the treatment of revenues from natural resources. The balance of the discussion seems to us to be that such revenues should be taken partially into account. The best practical way to do this is, we have concluded, to adjust the equalization which would be payable, to any province having natural resource revenue above the national average, by deducting an amount arrived at as follows: one half of the extent by which the natural resource revenue per capita exceeds the national average, multiplied by the population of the province.
It is estimated that the additional equalization payments under this formula will amount next year to about $55 million.
We also propose one further change in fiscal arrangements for the coming year. The abatement of federal succession duties, which has remained unchanged at 50 per cent since its inception, will be increased to 75 per cent though this increase will not be taken into account in calculating equalization. The cost to the federal treasury of this change is estimated at $32 million.
As noted in the Prime Minister's statement, the proposal is to return to the basis of equalization established in 1956; that is, to equalize the per capita return of the standard taxes in all provinces up to the level of the average per capita return in the two provinces having the highest yield. This equalization to the top two provinces is to replace the present system of equalization based on the national average.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps it would be useful if I illustrated the actual difference, in per capita terms, between the national average yield of standard taxes and the yield in the top two provinces. For the current year 1964-65, at the present rates of standard

Dominion-Provincial Relations taxes-that is, 18, 9, 50-the estimated national average yield is $42.61 per capita, whereas the average yield in the top two provinces, Ontario and British Columbia, is estimated at $54.92 per capita. It can be seen, therefore, that setting aside the effect of the national resource component of the equalization formula, raising a province's yield to the level of the top two, rather than to the national average, means an additional $12.31 per capita. I think it is hardly necessary to say that this matter of equalization is of fundamental importance in the fiscal arrangements between the federal and provincial governments, because the poorer provinces depend to a considerable extent upon some such system of fiscal adjustments to enable them to supply the services for which they are responsible under the constitution. If the equalization system is inadequate, the poorer provinces will be unduly burdened in their attempt to maintain reasonable standards in the public services for which they are responsible; and if they fail to maintain a reasonable standard of essential services, the national interest is affected.
Having said that, I should add that the argument for the equalization of the standard taxes to the level of the top two provinces does not rest on grounds of fairness or broad national interest alone. The provincial origins of the incomes and accumulations of wealth upon which income tax and estate tax yields depend are often widespread and are rarely known with accuracy. This in itself would, I suggest, support the view that some portion of their yield ought to be equalized among the various provinces. But while we believe that equalization of the standard income and estate taxes to the level of the yield in the top two provinces is of vital importance in the maintenance of a healthy federal system, we recognize that other factors have a significant effect on fiscal capacity, and in particular we recognize that there are wide variations in provincial natural resources revenue.
For example, for the year 1961-62 the average natural resources revenue per capita ranges from a low of 15 cents per capita in Prince Edward Island to a high of $94.08 per capita in Alberta. For the other provinces it is as follows: Newfoundland, $3.04; Nova Scotia, $1.84; New Brunswick, $6.52; Quebec, $6.62; Ontario, $6.91; Manitoba, $4.50; Saskatchewan, $22.57; and British Columbia, $37.72. Accordingly, while we believe in an equalization formula which will raise the level of the standard taxes up to the level of the

top two provinces, we also believe that the need for equalization is reduced in provinces that receive natural resources revenue above the national average. That is why the equalization formula which was proposed to the provinces and is now to be recommended to parliament will include a deduction for natural resources revenue in excess of the national average. This deduction will be equal to one half of the per capita amount by which the three year average of a province's natural resources revenue exceeds the per capita national average natural resources revenue, multiplied by the population of that province.
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend suggested that if I made this statement tonight he might have a chance to read it, and I agreed with him earlier that this was a highly complex calculation. At the present time this deduction would affect the provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan, all of which have natural resources revenues in excess of the national average.
Mr. Chairman, I have just finished a brief description of one item that will be included under the resolution and will be provided for in the bill. There are a number of other items that I should like to explain to the committee, but perhaps rather than start on any others tonight we might agree to call it 10.30.

I think we probably all agree, Mr. Chairman, that this a good thing to do. I will read this as fast as I can.
The statement made by the Prime Minister at the November conference also included the proposal to raise the provincial share of the estate tax from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. The Estate Tax Act was subsequently amended to make an abatement of 75 per cent available to provinces levying their own succession duties. At the present time, British Columbia is the only province in which the 75 per cent abatement from the federal rate is in effect. For the current year, the rate of abatement in effect in Ontario and Quebec is 50 per cent. It is proposed that these two provinces receive an additional 25 per cent of the estate tax in the form of a payment from the federal government. This arrangement was preferred in Ontario and Quebec pending the findings of their tax commissions. The other seven provinces now receive 50 per cent of the yield of the federal estate tax in the form of a payment from the federal government and it is proposed that they receive an additional payment equal to 25 per cent of the federal estate tax.
We made it clear at the November conference that we recognized the increasing burden falling on the provinces because of the rising cost of providing high priority services such as education, and we agreed to do something immediately to ease these burdens. It was understood that a further careful examination of the whole problem would be made with a view to seeing if an adjustment of more substantial kind should be attempted for the next fiscal arrangements period commencing April 1, 1967. However, following further consideration growing out of the discussions at the federal-provincial conference in Quebec city, March 31 to April 2, it was decided that in recognition of the increasing financial needs of the provinces, we should not wait until 1967 before making additional financial resources available to them.
The result of this further consideration was a decision to recommend to parliament that the rate of abatement of the federal individual income tax be increased by an additional two percentage points in the taxation year 1965 and by an additional four percentage points
Dominion-Provincial Relations in 1966 above the level which would have prevailed under the existing legislation. The additional abatements have already been provided for by amendment of section 33 of the Income Tax Act as a result of Bill No. C-91 which received royal assent on June 18. It remains to make the parallel amendment to the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act so that the standard individual income tax rates will be the same as the rates of abatement. This is necessary so that the level of equalization will be brought into line with the level of the standard abatement. Under the existing legislation-that is, under the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act -the standard individual income tax rises by one percentage point in each of the five years of the agreement period. The standard tax was 16 per cent of the gross federal tax for the taxation year 1962, 17 per cent for the taxation year 1963, 18 per cent for the current taxation year 1964, would rise to 19 per cent for 1965 and to 20 per cent in 1966, the final year of the present period. Under the proposed legislation the standard tax will be 21 per cent for the taxation year 1965, rather than 19, and 24 per cent for the taxation year 1966, rather than the 20 per cent which is now provided for in the legislation. The effect of the increase in the levels of abatement under the Income Tax Act is that any province which chooses to increase its own income tax rates by like amount will be able to obtain the additional revenue from the two percentage points in 1965 and from the four percentage points in 1966 without raising the over-all level of individual income tax. The effect of the increase in the standard tax is to increase the amounts of equalization in line with these higher abatements. In other words, the value of the increased abatement will by this means be equalized to the yield in the top two provinces.
In order that the committee may know the financial importance of the measures which we recommend, I should like permission to place on Hansard at this point a table showing the estimated increase in provincial revenues for the fiscal years 1964-65, 1965-66 and 1966-67 which will flow from the implementation of these proposals. If there is unanimous consent I should like to table them now.

speechtext:
This table indicates that tor the fiscal year 1964-65 it is estimated that changing to the top two bases ot equalization will bring the provinces an additional $55.3 million and the value of an additional 25 per cent of the estate tax will be $32.2 million, or a total of $87.5 million. For the year 1965-66 it is estimated that the provinces will be $171.2 million better off than under the arrangements now in effect, the proposals made at the November 1963 conference accounting for $106.6 million of this increase and an additional two percentage points of the individual income tax proposed following the Quebec conference accounting for $64.6 million. It is estimated that for the fiscal year 1966-67, the final year of the present fiscal arrangements period, the provinces will be some $265 million better off than they would have been under the present arrangements.
The proposed changes in the fiscal arrangements with the provinces involve both the system of equalization and the amount of the federal abatement and are the two major adjustments of the fiscal arrangements referred to in the resolution. As noted above, they will result in rising financial benefits to the provinces, culminating in an annual gain to them of some $265 million in 1966-67 including the increased abatement already provided under the Income Tax Act. I submit this is a very generous recognition of the financial problems of the provincial governments, Mr. Chairman, and when viewed in the light of the federal government's own sizeable deficits it illustrates in dramatic fashion the government's belief in co-operative federalism.
I should perhaps add a word or two about the effect of these changes on the budgetary position of the federal government. In my budget speech of March 16 last I forecast a deficit for the current fiscal year of $455 million according to the traditional method of accounting. Transfers to the provinces of the amounts contemplated, $265 million on an annual basis in 1966-67, will be bound to increase the federal deficit.
Hon. members know that a very high proportion of the federal government's total expenditures are fixed or uncontrollable if we include defence expenditures and social security payments in the fixed or uncontrollable category. Capital expenditures, for example, which are controllable are estimated at only $268 million for the current year, which is 4 per cent of total expenditures for the year. It is sometimes suggested
Dominion-Provincial Relations this is an area that could be dealt with differently, but as a percentage of the total it is only 4 per cent. In other words, while we are making every effort to keep expenditures in check, the scope for cutting them appreciably or very considerably is not nearly as great as many people think. I mention this to emphasize the problem created for the federal government by the contemplated reduction in its revenues of $265 million a year in order to help the provinces meet their financial difficulties. Obviously there must be limits beyond which the federal government cannot go without endangering its own financial position, and I trust this will be recognized by the provinces as well as by those of us who are in the federal parliament, because to be successful co-operative federalism must work both ways.
While the proposed changes in the system of equalization and the increase in the federal abatement of the individual income tax are the most important of the fiscal revisions that are proposed, the bill will contain a number of other fiscal revisions which are of varying degrees of importance to the provinces. It is proposed that the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act be amended to permit the use of the one year option for the determination of the succession duty rental applicable in the provinces of Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Manitoba for the years 1957-58 to 1961-62.
This provision will give effect to an undertaking made by two previous administrations but never given statutory authority. Under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, chapter 29, 4-5 Elizabeth II, the standard sucession duty applicable to a province for a given year is equal to 50 per cent of the three year average of the succession duties payable on the estates of persons dying in that year and the two preceding years. During the course of the negotiations preceding the signing of the tax rental agreements, it was argued that a renting province should be given the option of a one year basis since in fact a province which did not rent received the 50 per cent abatement on the one year basis.
The then Minister of Finance undertook to secure the authority to make the one year option possible. The undertaking was first extended to the province of British Columbia by letter of February 14, 1957, and subsequently to the province of Saskatchewan by letter of May 17, 1957, and to the province of Manitoba by letter of October 30, 1957. The

Dominion-Provincial Relations other five provinces which rented the succession duty field to Canada were asked by the then minister of finance in letters dated April 24, 1958, whether they wished to avail themselves of the one year option.
No other provinces indicated their desire to avail themselves of the one year option, and on the basis of that inquiry it has therefore been limited to the provinces which requested it, namely British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
The passage of this particular provision will discharge a commitment previously given and will enable us to bring finality to the calculation of the succession duty rentals for those three provinces for the relevant years. It is not possible to tell in advance whether the selection of a one year basis for a succession duty rental would benefit a particular province for a given five year period. If some particularly wealthy person or persons had died in the two year period immediately preceding the agreements, a three year average might benefit a province. Conversely, if succession duties were tending to rise year by year, the one year basis might benefit a province. Because the one year basis will produce different results than the three year average, the option is naturally limited to those provinces which made their choice known at the beginning of the period.
A further provision of the proposed legislation has to do with the recommendations of the royal commission on Newfoundland finances appointed under term 29 of the terms of union. At the present time the payment of $8 million per annum recommended by the royal commission on Newfoundland finances is made under section 3(3) of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act and the authority to pay this amount extends to March 31, 1967. It is proposed that the $8 million per annum be made payable to the province of Newfoundland in accordance with the recommendation of the royal commission on Newfoundland finances without specifying any terminal date.
Another provision has to do with the Crown Corporations (Provincial Taxes and Fees) Act which was given royal assent on June 18, 1964. In accordance with the provisions of that legislation certain federal crown corporations listed in the schedule to the act are required to pay provincial retail sales taxes, gasoline taxes and motor vehicle licences, with effect from April 1, 1964. This legislation was first proposed in 1962 under the previous government, and it was the intention at that time that the affected corporations should pay the

specified provincial taxes from April 1, 1962. The legislation was never introduced, but the matter has been on the order paper on a number of occasions. While it was thought wrong at this time to give retroactive effect to this legislation, the government does not want the provinces to lose financially-I am referring to the bill that was passed some weeks ago-from the fact that events over which they had no control intervened in such a way as to make it impossible to carry out the original intention. It was more than an intention; it was more or less a commitment. Consequently it is proposed that an estimate be made of the taxes that would have been paid had the legislation been in effect from April 1, 1962 to March 31, 1964 and that such estimated amounts be paid to the provinces. It will come to about $6 million in total for the two years in question.
There is one further matter of importance that will be dealt with in the bill, that is, in the words of the resolution "To provide adjustment of fiscal arrangements and taxation provisions consequential upon the provision of youth allowances to parents resident in certain provinces". The bill dealing with the provision of the youth allowances has now been passed. The house is therefore familiar with the fact that it is not the intention to pay federal youth allowances in a province that provides its own system of schooling allowances on a basis similar to the federal plan. It is proposed that in such a province the federal income tax be reduced by a further 3 percentage points. This requires an amendment to provide an additional abatement of 3 percentage points under section 33 of the Income Tax Act. In provinces in which the federal youth allowances are paid it is proposed that the abatement under section 33 of the Income Tax Act be 21 per cent of the basic federal tax for the taxation year 1965 and in provinces which provide their own schooling allowances, 24 per cent of the basic federal tax.
The value of an additional abatement of 3 per cent in the federal income tax may be more or less than the value of the schooling allowances provided by the province. It is not intended that a province should be better off or worse off as a result of its decision to provide its own system of schooling allowances. If federal revenues decline more by reason of granting the additional 3 per cent abatement in a province providing its own system of schooling allowances than it would have cost the federal government to provide

the youth allowances in the province, we will recover this net loss from that province.
Conversely, if federal revenues are estimated to have declined less as a result of providing the additional 3 per cent abatement of federal individual income tax in a province providing its own system of schooling allowances than it would have cost the federal government to provide the youth allowances in that province, the federal government will pay this difference in cost to the province. Provision will be contained in the bill when it is before the committee for such adjustments.
I hope that the statement I have just made will provide a useful explanation of the subject matter covered by the resolution. The broad purpose is clear. It is to improve the financial position of the provinces and to contribute to order and harmony in federal provincial relations. The specific measures by which we achieve this broad purpose are, however, complex and difficult. I hope that my explanation of these matters has been sufficient but I shall be ready to amplify it later on in the course of debate.

TRADE-BEEF-STEPS TO INCREASE EXPORTS TO GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
The reason I asked my question today on orders of the day was twofold; there were two reasons for it. The first reason was in regard to the potential market in the United Kingdom for Canadian beef. Sometime ago, Canada did have a market for this type of beef in the United Kingdom and for some reason unknown we lost that market. It would seem to me that this is the ideal time for us to regain the market we had in the United Kingdom. It possibly is unfortunate that they had a drought in Argentina this past year and were unable to supply their customers.
From press reports I understand that the Americans have sent a shipment of beef to the United Kingdom. I noticed that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) in reply to a question put to him by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood) said that the Canadian trade commissioner in Great Britain was investigating this, and he referred to it as a problem. To me, it is not a problem. As Canadians we should not be considering it as a problem. The people in the United Kingdom-yes, they have a problem because their beef prices are so high.


He also said the spread was not great enough. From press reports we understand that special cuts of beef are selling in the United Kingdom for $2 a pound. Similar cuts are selling in Canada at the present time for 79 cents. How much of a spread do you want? I realize these are probably the best cuts, but proportionately the spread should be the same all the way down. Certainly with the devaluation of the Canadian dollar our beef should again be in the running for that market. I ask the parliamentary secretary, what efforts have his department made to regain this market?
My second reason for asking this question has to do with a threatened drought this year in the northern part of the prairies. It may not develop, but unless we get rain very quickly farmers will be forced to sell their cattle herds. Unlike the southern part of the prairie provinces, where provision has been made for such catastrophes because they have had them in the past, the northern part of the prairies has seldom experienced such a catastrophe. They are not prepared for carrying over their herds; they are not prepared by having reserve feed, and they may be forced to settle their problem in one of two ways. They will either have to ship their cattle to the southern part of the province, which is very costly, or they will have to flood the market with this beef.
The department knows what will happen if the market is flooded. Prices will be depressed and this affects the economy of all Canada. I am sure we do not want this to happen. I am also thinking of the future in this connection. Canada is capable of producing much more beef than she can consume, and with the advent of ARDA and the proposed opening of new grazing lands in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, we can produce much more beef. If we do produce more beef, we must have markets in which to sell it. I would ask the department to do everything they possibly can to regain part of this market, bearing in mind that the Americans have already sent trial shipments to Great Britain, that we had this market on a prior occasion, and that there is a special process by which this beef can be prepared for shipment. It can be sent to the United Kingdom in refrigerated cars and ships. I understand that this special process does not require too much preparation. They strip the hides off the cattle, chill the beef and ship it. I realize that we cannot send live cattle over there because it is too costly. But this market was open to beef shippers in Canada before,

and I think this is a golden opportunity for Canada to recapture the market.
I hope the department will consider what I have suggested and that they have already had results from the investigation which the minister said he had under way when he was asked about this on a former occasion.

speechtext:
Montreal, June 22, 1964. Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
We write to apprise you of a situation developing which may bring about a suspension of railway services in Canada.
On May 20, 1964, the Munroe conciliation board, appointed by the Minister of Labour to inquire into a dispute between the railways and their non-operating employees, submitted a majority report recommending wage increases during 1964 and 1965 totalling approximately 19.1 cents per hour or $32.50 per employee per month. This would add to the wage bills of Canadian National and Canadian Pacific amounts estimated at $18.2 million for 1964, $39.0 million for 1965 and $46.3 million for each succeeding year.
This was the latest of a series of conciliation board reports which have dealt with disputes between the railways and their nonoperating employees on a biennial basis since world war II. Between 1946 and 1959 these employees secured increases in wages, fringe benefits, or both, on seven successive occasions. To cover the added costs involved, the railways applied to and received authority from the board of transport commissioners to make general increases in freight rates, the last of which was an increase of 17 per cent effective December 1, 1958. Because this series of general freight rate increases gave rise to allegations of discrimination and inequities in the freight rate structure, in March, 1959, the government announced that no further general increases in freight rates would be permitted pending study by a royal commission to be appointed to inquire into railway transportation in Canada. On May 13, 1959, the MacPherson royal commission was appointed under terms set forth in P.C. 1959-577.
Subsequently parliament enacted the Freight Rates Reduction Act with effect from August 1, 1959, under which the 17 per cent increase in freight rates of December 1, 1958, was rolled back to 10 per cent and the sum
of $20 million per annum was provided to compensate the railways for the loss of revenues therefrom. On May 2, 1960, by order of the board of transport commissioners, the 17 per cent increase was further rolled back from 10 per cent to 8 per cent.
In 1960 the non-operating employees made further demands upon the railways. The conciliation board which dealt with that dispute recommended wage increases totalling some 14 cents per hour together with improved vacation benefits. The railways rejected the report and a strike called for December 3, 1960, was averted by parliament which passed the Railway Operation Continuation Act preventing strike action until May 15, 1961. In the meantime, in March, 1961, the MacPherson royal commission submitted the first volume of its report. The government decided, pending receipt of the complete report, to make interim payments to the railways related to the recommendations of the royal commission in the amount of $50 million per annum. The dispute between the railways and the non-operating employees was settled on the basis of the majority report of the conciliation board and the Railway Operation Continuation Act lapsed.
The second volume of the MacPherson royal commission report was released in January, 1962. In the meantime, the nonoperating employees had made further demands in respect of the years 1962-63. That dispute was settled on the basis of the unanimous report of a conciliation board which added 9 cents per hour to railway payroll costs. The railways accepted the report and undertook the added costs involved which, together with increases accorded running trades employees, totalled some $31.7 million on a recurring annual basis, in anticipation of legislative action to implement the recommendations of the royal commission. As you are aware, such action has been repeatedly delayed.
In the meantime, however, government has further circumscribed the ability of the railways to raise added revenues to meet increased costs and, indeed, has impaired their sources of revenues. On May 7, 1959, by order in council P.C. 1959-569, the authority

granted by the board of transport commissioners, sustained on appeal by the Supreme Court of Canada, to apply demurrage charges on cars loaded with grain consigned to terminal elevators in western Canada, was suspended and has remained so ever since. By an amendment to the Railway Act, on August 1, 1961, the statutory rates covering the movement of grain and grain products in western Canada enacted by parliament in 1925, were made applicable to rapeseed as well. This was done after the board of transport commissioners had dismissed an application that rapeseed be classed as grain. As a result, this artificially low level of rates which is applicable to so large a segment of the railways' traffic and which has become increasingly onerous in the face of rising costs, was not only continued but, indeed, extended with impairment to the revenue position of the railways. On March 30, 1961, by order in council P.C. 1961-497, increases in the at-and-east grain rates authorized by the board of transport commissioners which found the rates in effect to be below cost, were suspended. Successive orders in council have continued this suspension, currently until December 31, 1964.
Throughout the post-war period the railways have necessarily had to accord operating and other employees increases in wages and fringe benefits generally comparable to those secured by the non-operating employees. Recently material prices which had been relatively stable for some time have started to move upwards.
Incidentally, although the railways have continued in effect the reductions in freight rates brought about by the Freight Rates Reduction Act, and while the government has given assurance of its intention to place before parliament the matter of payments at the same rate as last year, this has not yet been done and the railways have not been in receipt of interim payments since December 31, 1963, or payments in respect of the Freight Rates Reduction Act since March 31, 1964.
More recently, the Minister of Transport has stated that no branch line abandonments in western Canada will be permitted pending enactment of legislation based on the Mac-Pherson royal commission report.
Thus the railways find themselves by the action of government deprived of authority to raise added revenues to meet increased costs and circumscribed in their ability to
effect economies through the discontinuance of unremunerative operations. Under these conditions, they cannot undertake the responsibility of assuming added costs of the magnitude implicit in the majority report of the Munroe conciliation board.
Even though rejection of the report may inevitably lead to a railway strike, existing circumstances leave us no alternative. Before taking this action, however, we felt the matter should be placed before you. We will be available for a meeting with you to explore the situation further if that should be desired.
Yours truly,
D. Gordon,
Chairman and president Canadian National Railways
N. R. Crump,
Chairman and president Canadian Pacific Railway Company
The Rt. Hon. L. B. Pearson,
Prime Minister,
Ottawa 4, Ont.
The following communication was directed by the Prime Minister to the presidents of the railways in reply to their letter of June 22, 1964.
Canadian National Telecommunications Ottawa, June 30, 1964.
The letter which you sent forward on June 22, dealing with the wage negotiations between the railways and their non-operating employees and the report of the conciliation board on this matter, has been studied with great care. The federal government is aware of the difficulties for the railways which are inherent in this situation.
The government has indicated to you its firm intention to proceed with new railway legislation which will satisfy major objectives of the report of the MacPherson royal commission on transportation. At the same time, it is recognized that, while the resolution preceding introduction of this legislation is awaiting consideration by parliament, other items of parliamentary business must be dealt with first. This makes it likely that some time will pass before the MacPherson legislation can be considered by parliament.
In these special circumstances the government would undertake to review the situation in six months' time. This review would

take place in the light of an impartial examination of the costs of a wage settlement by the railways in the situation described in your letter, so that the government would be afforded an opportunity to decide what
additional temporary financial adjustments would be justified to assist the railways during the period up to the coming into effect of the proposed new railway legislation.
L. B. Pearson.
Wednesday, July 8, 1964
